37.0.big: An ecosystem is a community of living things plus their nonliving surroundings. Energy flows through it one way, and matter cycles around and around.
points: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat. Carbon, nitrogen, water and other elements are recycled.

37.1.big: Ecosystems are studied as webs of feeding relationships, and scientists test them with experiments and models.
points: Resistance = staying the same despite a disturbance. Resilience = how fast it recovers. A steady state is equilibrium. The study of how ecosystems change is ecosystem dynamics.
A food chain is one linear path. A food web shows all the connections (more realistic). A trophic level is a step on the chain.
Primary producers (plants, algae, phytoplankton; in the dark, chemoautotrophs) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers → apex consumers at the top.
Grazing food web: starts with living plants. Detrital food web: starts with dead material and decomposers.
Experiments: a mesocosm fences off part of the real ecosystem. A microcosm rebuilds a mini-ecosystem in the lab. Both may not behave exactly like the real thing.

Models: a conceptual model (flow chart), an analytical model (math equations for simple, linear systems), a simulation model (computer programs for complex systems), and a holistic ecosystem model (tries to include everything).

37.2.big: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level makes it to the next. The rest is lost as heat. That's why food chains are short.
points: Biomass = the mass of living things at a point in time.
Gross primary productivity = all the energy producers capture. Net primary productivity = that minus what they burn in respiration, which is what's actually available to consumers.

For consumers: assimilation = energy absorbed from food (not lost in feces). Net consumer productivity = assimilated energy minus respiration. Net production efficiency (NPE) = net productivity ÷ assimilation.

Trophic level transfer efficiency (TLTE) = (production at this level ÷ production at the level below) × 100, usually about 10%. The second law of thermodynamics means some energy is always lost as heat.

Ecological pyramids: energy (never upside down, the most accurate), biomass (can flip: tiny, fast-reproducing phytoplankton in the English Channel), numbers (can flip: one tree feeding thousands of insects).
Biomagnification: toxins like DDT, PCBs and mercury build up in fat and get more concentrated at each level up, so top predators get the most.
37.2.tip: 10% rule: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kcal going up four levels.

37.3.big: Biogeochemical cycles move water, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur between living things, air, water and rock.
points: Water: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff, groundwater. Residence time = how long a molecule stays in one reservoir. All of Earth's water is the hydrosphere.

Carbon: photosynthesis pulls CO₂ out of the air, and respiration, decomposition and burning put it back. The oceans are the biggest carbon reservoir (dissolved carbon and rock). Fossil fuels are a non-renewable resource. Carbon also cycles through rock, as at subduction zones and volcanoes.
Nitrogen: bacteria fix N₂ from the air into ammonia (nitrogen fixation), nitrify it, and denitrify it back to N₂. Plants take up ammonium and nitrate.
Phosphorus: no gas form. It comes mainly from weathering rock, cycles through living things, and settles in ocean sediment. Often the limiting nutrient.
Too much N and P (fertilizer runoff) → eutrophication → algal blooms → decomposers use up oxygen → dead zones.
Sulfur: from volcanoes and burning fossil fuels as SO₂ → falls as sulfuric acid rain. Particles settling out of the air are fallout.

12.why: The second law of thermodynamics: every conversion loses some energy as heat.

13.why: Only about 10% passes up each level, so energy runs out after a few levels.

14.why: Energy pyramids always show the true structure (they never invert).

15.why: Phytoplankton reproduce so fast (high turnover) that a small standing crop feeds many consumers.

16.why: Making energy from inorganic chemicals without light = chemoautotrophs.

17.why: Turning N₂ into usable forms = nitrogen fixation.

20.why: Excess N and P → algal blooms → oxygen used up → a dead zone.

21.why: Water flowing over land after rain or snowmelt = surface runoff.

22.why: Carbon levels depend mostly on exchange between the atmosphere and water.

23.why: Each biome has lots of variation inside it that one label hides.

24.why: Fencing off (mesocosm) or rebuilding (microcosm) can change how the system behaves.

25.why: A simulation model uses computers to handle complex relationships.

26.why: Both show energy flow. Chains are linear and simple. Webs are non-linear, more accurate and holistic, and can feed simulation models.

27.why: Lightning (natural fire) and pollution (human) both alter ecosystems.

28.why: A small phytoplankton biomass supports a lot of zooplankton, so they must be very productive (they reproduce fast).

29.why: Few producers by number but huge biomass = big trees.

30.why: Number and biomass pyramids can invert: a summer temperate forest (numbers) and English Channel phytoplankton (biomass). Energy pyramids never do.

31.why: Producers burn some energy themselves, so NPP is what consumers actually get.

32.why: Adding nitrogen lowered species richness: some species outcompete others.

33.why: The deep ocean holds about 37,100 Gt of carbon: the oceans.

34.why: Sulfur dioxide leaves the air as sulfuric acid rain.

35.why: Excess producers die and decompose, and decomposers use up the oxygen.

36.why: Producers turn light into chemical energy by photosynthesis, and consumers eat them (or each other).

37.why: Larger dissolved carbon particles block light, so producers decrease.

38.why: Two species raised the dissolved carbon particle size, which blocked light and limited algae.

39.why: Producers are the base of the pyramid (D).

40.why: Without otters, the larger fish's growth and trophic position changed most. Small fish look about the same.

41.why: Coyotes lose deer and rabbits and must share voles, so their biomass drops sharply.

42.why: Row B feeds the top level. Lose it and the top predators starve, possibly collapsing the web.

44.why: Without predators, herbivores overate their food, then starved.

45.why: Too many consumers eat up the producers.

47.why: About 10% per step: 33,000 → 3,300 → 330 → ~33. Of the choices, 75 is the only plausible small value.

48.why: Decomposers feed on dead material from every level. Tertiary consumers eat only secondary consumers.

49.why: Photosynthesis pulls CO₂ out of the air.
